## 📏 Two measures: IRCA and Saber 11 {#water-measures}

::: {.cards .groups}
::: {}
[💧 IRCA · water-quality risk]{.group}

- 🧪 tap-water samples against health limits
- ⚖️ failed tests weighted by risk: *E. coli* 25 · turbidity 15 · pH 1.5
- 📏 0 = no risk → 100 = unfit
:::
::: {.fragment}
[🎓 Saber 11 · ICFES exam]{.group}

- 🧑‍🎓 students finishing secondary school
- 📚 5 tests: reading, maths, social studies, science, English
- 📏 global score 0–500
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .bigline}
🧮 both are averages: IRCA over water samples · Saber 11 over students
:::

[Resolución 2115 de 2007, arts. 13–14 ([normas.cra.gov.co](https://normas.cra.gov.co/gestor/docs/resolucion_minproteccion_2115_2007.htm)) ·
ICFES, *Saber 11.° Guía de orientación 2017-1*, pp. 101 and 104 ([icfes.gov.co](https://www.icfes.gov.co/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Guia-de-orientacion-saber-11-2017-1.pdf))]{.source}

::: {.notes}
IRCA (Índice de Riesgo de la Calidad del Agua para consumo humano), Resolución 2115 de
2007: each tested characteristic carries a risk score (art. 13, Cuadro 6: *Escherichia
coli* 25, total coliforms 15, turbidity 15, free residual chlorine 15, apparent colour 6,
pH 1.5, among others). A sample's IRCA is the score of the characteristics that fail their
limit as a percentage of the score of all characteristics analysed, and the monthly IRCA
is the mean over the month's samples (art. 14). So 0 means every test passed and 100 means
every test failed. Our `irca` is the year's utility-supplied ("prestadores") IRCA from the
INS open table; the next slide shows why that matters. Saber 11 is ICFES's standardized exam
for students finishing upper secondary school, with five tests (critical reading,
mathematics, social studies and citizenship, natural sciences, English). The global score
is 5 × the weighted mean of the five test scores (each 0–100; English weight 1, the others
3), on 0–500 without decimals, and its mean was fixed at 250 in the first sitting (2014-2)
so that years compare (guide, p. 104). Our `saber11_mean` is the mean global score of the
students whose school is in that municipality and zone, both sittings of a year pooled; it
covers only students who sat the exam, so it says nothing about those who left school.
Sources checked 2026-10-30.
:::

[INS IRCA for 2023: MinSalud, MinVivienda, INS and Superservicios, *INCA 2023* (Bogotá,
January 2025), Tabla 4 · bands: Resolución 2115 de 2007, art. 15
([normas.cra.gov.co](https://normas.cra.gov.co/gestor/docs/resolucion_minproteccion_2115_2007.htm))]{.source}

::: {.notes}
IRCA (Índice de Riesgo de la Calidad del Agua para consumo humano) scores the
surveillance samples of a year: 0 means no risk, 100 means unfit. The five cards are the
risk bands of Resolución 2115 de 2007 (Ministerio de la Protección Social and Ministerio de
Ambiente, Vivienda y Desarrollo Territorial), article 15:
https://normas.cra.gov.co/gestor/docs/resolucion_minproteccion_2115_2007.htm (verified by
the lead, 2026-10-30). The 2023 values land in their bands: MinSalud, MinVivienda, INS and
Superservicios, *Informe Nacional de Calidad del Agua para Consumo Humano INCA 2023*
(Bogotá, January 2025), Tabla 4 (INS IRCA 2023): Nacional 16.4, Prestadores 7.4,
Autoabastecedores 43.7, Urbano 5.7, Rural 36.5.
https://www.minvivienda.gov.co/sites/default/files/documentos/informe-nacional-de-calidad-del-agua-para-consumo-humano-inca-2023.pdf
(verified by the lead, 2026-10-30). Rural water in 2023 sits in the high-risk band on
average. The second fragment matters for our data: the open table we use (datos.gov.co
`nxt2-39c3`) holds the utility-supplied ("prestadores") IRCA, which is far lower than the
self-supplied systems' score, so our dataset understates the risk where no utility exists.
The same orange ramp, brighter for more risk on these dark slides, colours every IRCA band
chart in Part 2. The emoji are mnemonic only; the label carries the meaning.
:::

## 🧠 The question {#water-question}

::: {.bigline}
🧩 Which **kinds** of municipality exist?
:::

. . .

::: {.bigline}
🎯 How do 👶 health and 🎓 education outcomes **differ** between them?
:::

::: {.notes}
"Kinds" are clusters found by k-means on water quality, services and context. The unit is a
municipality's urban or rural zone in one year, so a municipality's two zones can belong to
different kinds, and a zone can move between kinds over the years. Outcomes are compared
between kinds, not used to find them.
:::

::: {.notes}
Columns: `irca` (utility-supplied, prestadores IRCA), `water_coverage`, `sewer_coverage`, `ipm` (2018 census), `rural_share`,
`altitude_m` (derived SRTM point), `rainfall_mm` (CHIRPS), `mdm` (from 2016) and
`sgp_water_pc` (nominal pesos per person, log-transformed). Outcomes: `infant_mortality`
(municipal), `saber11_mean` (zone) and `dropout_rate` (municipal). Clustering on an outcome
would make the comparison circular: the clusters would differ on it by construction. The
fiscal index `idf` is left out because its method changes in 2020 (`idf_new`). The three
groups are for reading only: k-means sees nine z-scored columns with equal weight.
:::

## 🔁 Compute once, publish many {#water-compute-once}

::: {.wat-flow}
```text
data/water_municipal.csv
        │   uv run python scripts/analysis.py
        ▼
outputs/clusters.parquet  +  outputs/cluster_profiles.csv
        │   every page reads them
        ▼
explore · clusters · report · slides · blog · dashboard
```
:::

::: {.bigline}
🧮 compute once → 📤 never copy a number by hand
:::

::: {.notes}
One importable script (`scripts/analysis.py`) does all the computation and writes
`outputs/`. Pages only read and draw. Change a design choice once and every output follows
at the next render. This deck imports the same script and computes in memory, so it does
not need `outputs/`. Parquet keeps column types (text codes stay text); CSV is easy to open
anywhere.
:::

## 🌾 Rural: less data, more risk {#water-bands}

```{python}
#| label: fig-wat-bands
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "All rows, 2010–2023, by zone: no IRCA reported (hatched grey) and Resolución 2115 risk band. Utility-supplied (prestadores) IRCA, INS open data nxt2-39c3."
#| fig-alt: "Two horizontal stacked bars, urban and rural. The urban bar is mostly no-risk and low-risk IRCA with a small hatched no-data share. The rural bar is more than half hatched no-data, and the largest share of the rest is in the high-risk band."
wat_bandcat = wat_analysis.irca_band(wat_raw["irca"]).astype(str).where(wat_raw["irca"].notna(), "No IRCA")
wat_order = ["No IRCA"] + wat_analysis.IRCA_BANDS
wat_tab = wat_pd.crosstab(wat_raw["zone"], wat_bandcat).reindex(columns=wat_order, fill_value=0)
wat_tab = wat_tab.reindex(["rural", "urban"])
wat_pct = wat_tab.div(wat_tab.sum(axis=1), axis=0) * 100
wat_rural_missing = f"{wat_pct.loc['rural', 'No IRCA']:.0f}%"
wat_rural_high = wat_tab.loc["rural", ["High", "Unfit"]].sum() / wat_tab.loc["rural", wat_analysis.IRCA_BANDS].sum()
wat_rural_high = f"{wat_rural_high:.0%}"
with wat_plt.rc_context(wat_rc):
    wat_f, wat_ax = wat_plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 2.9))
    wat_left = wat_np.zeros(2)
    wat_cols = [wat_analysis.NO_DATA_COLOR["dark"]] + wat_analysis.BAND_COLORS["dark"]
    for wat_band, wat_col in zip(wat_order, wat_cols):
        wat_nodata = wat_band == "No IRCA"
        wat_ax.barh(["rural", "urban"], wat_pct[wat_band],
                    left=wat_left, color=wat_col, height=0.62, label=wat_band,
                    hatch=wat_analysis.NO_DATA_HATCH if wat_nodata else None,
                    edgecolor=wat_analysis.NO_DATA_EDGE["dark"] if wat_nodata else "#191919",
                    linewidth=0 if wat_nodata else 2)
        wat_left += wat_pct[wat_band].to_numpy()
    wat_ax.set_xlim(0, 100)
    wat_ax.set_xlabel("Share of rows (%)")
    wat_ax.legend(ncol=6, loc="lower left", bbox_to_anchor=(0, 1.0), fontsize=13,
                  handlelength=1.2, columnspacing=1.2)
    wat_plt.show()
```

❔ rural rows without IRCA: **`{python} wat_rural_missing`** · 🔴 rural rows with IRCA
in high or unfit: **`{python} wat_rural_high`**

::: {.notes}
Computed from all `{python} wat_fmt(wat_n_rows)` rows of `water_municipal.csv`, 2010–2023, including
non-municipalised areas (they are mostly empty). Many rural systems are never sampled, so
missingness is not random: it is concentrated in small, remote and rural places. IRCA is
the utility-supplied (prestadores) IRCA. The rural median also drops sharply in 2016 and
2020; the data README warns the 2020 drop may reflect which systems were sampled.
:::

## 🧹 Four steps from table to features {#water-prepare-steps}

::: {.cards}
::: {}
[✂️]{.big}

**select** 2016–2023 · municipalities · with IRCA
:::
::: {.fragment}
[🔄]{.big}

**transform** log SGP · capitals use the municipal total 🚩
:::
::: {.fragment}
[🩹]{.big}

**impute** year × zone median 🚩
:::
::: {.fragment}
[📏]{.big}

**standardise** z-score within year
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .bigline}
🚩 = a flag column, so nothing is filled silently
:::

::: {.notes}
Select: years 2016–2023 because MDM starts in 2016; municipalities only (San Andrés has no
TerriData values; non-municipalised areas are nearly empty); rows with IRCA only.
Transform: SGP per person is skewed, so take its log. Department capitals have no
urban/rural coverage split, so their urban rows use `water_coverage_total` /
`sewer_coverage_total` with a `*_from_total` flag; their rural rows are imputed like any
other gap. Impute: rows
missing more than two features are dropped; the rest get the year × zone median with a
`<feature>_imputed` flag. Standardise within each year: this removes the drift of nominal
pesos and year-level shifts, so one pooled k-means gives labels that are comparable over
time.
:::

## 📏 Why scale? {#water-scaling}

```{python}
#| label: fig-wat-scale
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Share of the squared distance between rows that each feature contributes, in raw units and after z-scores (kept rows, 2016–2023)."
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal bar chart with nine features. In raw units, rainfall and altitude together make up almost all of the distance and the other seven bars are invisible. After z-scores every feature contributes the same share, about 11 percent."
wat_var = wat_res["prepared"][wat_analysis.FEATURES].var(ddof=0)
wat_raw_share = (wat_var / wat_var.sum() * 100).sort_values()
wat_top2 = f"{wat_raw_share[['rainfall_mm', 'altitude_m']].sum():.1f}%"
wat_equal = 100 / len(wat_analysis.FEATURES)
with wat_plt.rc_context(wat_rc):
    wat_f, wat_ax = wat_plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 4.3))
    wat_y = wat_np.arange(len(wat_raw_share))
    wat_ax.barh(wat_y + 0.2, wat_raw_share, height=0.38, color=wat_analysis.BAND_COLORS["dark"][3],
                label="raw units")
    wat_ax.barh(wat_y - 0.2, wat_equal, height=0.38, color=wat_accent, label="z-scores")
    for wat_i, wat_v in enumerate(wat_raw_share):
        if wat_v >= 1:
            wat_ax.text(wat_v + 0.8, wat_i + 0.2, f"{wat_v:.0f}%", va="center", fontsize=13,
                        color=wat_muted)
    wat_ax.text(wat_equal + 1.2, wat_y[-3] - 0.2, f"z-scores: {wat_equal:.0f}% each", va="center",
                fontsize=13, color=wat_accent)
    wat_ax.text(wat_equal + 1.2, wat_y[2] + 0.2, "raw units: < 1% each", va="center",
                fontsize=13, color=wat_analysis.BAND_COLORS["dark"][3])
    wat_ax.set_yticks(wat_y, [wat_analysis.SHORT_LABELS[wat_c] for wat_c in wat_raw_share.index])
    wat_ax.set_xlabel("Share of squared distance (%)")
    wat_ax.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=13)
    wat_plt.show()
```

⛰️🌧️ raw units: altitude + rainfall = **`{python} wat_top2`** of the distance

::: {.notes}
k-means groups rows by Euclidean distance. A feature's share of the squared distance is
proportional to its variance, so in raw units the features measured in thousands (mm of
rain, metres of altitude) drown out IRCA, coverage and poverty. Z-scores give each feature
variance 1. Computed from the kept rows with `log_sgp_water_pc`; with raw pesos, SGP alone
would dominate.
:::

## 🧩 k-means in four steps {#water-kmeans}

```{python}
#| label: fig-wat-kmeans
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Synthetic toy points, not the water data: k-means with k = 3."
#| fig-alt: "Four small scatter panels of the same synthetic toy points. Panel 1: grey points and three cross-shaped starting centres. Panel 2: each point coloured by its nearest centre. Panel 3: centres moved to the mean of their points, with arrows. Panel 4: the final, stable clusters."
wat_rng = wat_np.random.default_rng(7)
wat_toy = wat_np.vstack([wat_rng.normal(m, 0.55, size=(40, 2))
                         for m in ([0, 0], [3, 0.6], [1.4, 2.8])])
wat_cent = wat_toy[[3, 5, 8]].copy()          # three starting points, deliberately poor


def wat_assign(wat_points, wat_centres):
    return ((wat_points[:, None, :] - wat_centres[None]) ** 2).sum(-1).argmin(1)


wat_lab1 = wat_assign(wat_toy, wat_cent)
wat_cent2 = wat_np.array([wat_toy[wat_lab1 == j].mean(0) for j in range(3)])
wat_cent_final = wat_cent2.copy()
for wat_iter in range(20):
    wat_lab_final = wat_assign(wat_toy, wat_cent_final)
    wat_cent_final = wat_np.array([wat_toy[wat_lab_final == j].mean(0) for j in range(3)])
wat_toy_cols = wat_np.array(wat_analysis.CLUSTER_COLORS[:3])
wat_steps = ["① drop k centres", "② assign to nearest", "③ move to the mean", "④ repeat → stable"]
with wat_plt.rc_context(wat_rc):
    wat_f, wat_axes = wat_plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(11.5, 3.3), sharex=True, sharey=True)
    for wat_i, wat_ax in enumerate(wat_axes):
        if wat_i == 0:
            wat_ax.scatter(*wat_toy.T, s=18, color="#7d8590")
            wat_c = wat_cent
        elif wat_i in (1, 2):
            wat_ax.scatter(*wat_toy.T, s=18, color=wat_toy_cols[wat_lab1])
            wat_c = wat_cent if wat_i == 1 else wat_cent2
        else:
            wat_ax.scatter(*wat_toy.T, s=18, color=wat_toy_cols[wat_lab_final])
            wat_c = wat_cent_final
        if wat_i == 2:
            for wat_a, wat_b in zip(wat_cent, wat_cent2):
                wat_ax.annotate("", wat_b, wat_a, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="white", lw=1.5))
        wat_ax.scatter(*wat_c.T, marker="X", s=180, color="white", edgecolor="#191919", linewidth=1.5)
        wat_ax.set_title(wat_steps[wat_i], fontsize=14, loc="left")
        wat_ax.set_xticks([])
        wat_ax.set_yticks([])
        wat_ax.spines[["left", "bottom"]].set_color("#4a4f55")
    wat_f.tight_layout()
    wat_plt.show()
```

::: {.bigline}
✕ = centre · 🎯 goal: points close to their centre
:::

::: {.fragment}
💧 water data: **k = `{python} wat_k`** is a hyperparameter, picked from
k = `{python} int(wat_ktab.index.min())`–`{python} int(wat_ktab.index.max())` by elbow + silhouette
:::

::: {.notes}
Synthetic toy points, labelled as such: 120 random points around three centres, drawn by
this deck with a fixed seed. k-means needs k up front. It starts from k centres, assigns
each point to the nearest, moves each centre to the mean of its points, and repeats until
nothing changes. Different starts can end in different solutions, so we run 20 starts
(`n_init=20`) and keep the best, with a fixed `random_state` for reproducibility. Inertia is
the sum of squared distances from points to their centre.

Choosing k for the water data (`choose_k()` in `analysis.py`, fitted on all kept rows):
k = 2 is excluded because it mostly splits urban from rural rows (adjusted Rand index with
the zone `{python} f"{wat_ktab.loc[2, 'ari_vs_zone']:.2f}"`). Elbow: take the smallest k ≥ 3 after which one more cluster cuts inertia
by less than 10%, if its silhouette is within 0.01 of the best k ≥ 3. Here the next cluster
cuts inertia by only `{python} f"{wat_ktab['inertia_drop'].get(wat_k + 1, 0.0):.0%}"` and the
silhouette (−1 to 1, on a fixed sample of 5,000 rows) is
`{python} f"{wat_ktab.loc[wat_k, 'silhouette']:.3f}"`. A silhouette near 0.2 is weak: the
kinds overlap and summarise a continuum, which is normal for social data. Stability:
refits with `{python} len(wat_analysis.STABILITY_SEEDS)` other seeds give the same clusters
(adjusted Rand index ≥ `{python} wat_analysis.floor_to(wat_s["ari_min"])`; 1 means perfect
agreement). The elbow and silhouette plots are on `clusters.qmd`.
:::

## 🫧 A picture of the clusters {#water-pca}

```{python}
#| label: fig-wat-pca
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Each dot is a zone-year on the first two principal components of the 9 z-scored features, coloured by cluster. PCA is only for the picture; k-means used all 9 features."
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of about eleven thousand dots in four coloured groups that overlap at their edges. Cluster 4 spreads to the right, cluster 1 to the lower left and cluster 2 to the upper left; cluster 3 sits in the middle, drawn on top."
with wat_plt.rc_context(wat_rc):
    wat_f, wat_ax = wat_plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 4.9))
    # Outer clusters first, so the central one (cluster 3) is drawn on top, not hidden.
    wat_centres = wat_clusters.groupby("cluster")[["pc1", "pc2"]].mean()
    wat_order_pca = (wat_centres ** 2).sum(axis=1).sort_values(ascending=False).index
    wat_handles = {}
    for wat_c in wat_order_pca:
        wat_g = wat_clusters[wat_clusters["cluster"] == wat_c]
        wat_handles[wat_c] = wat_ax.scatter(
            wat_g["pc1"], wat_g["pc2"], s=6, color=wat_colors[wat_c],
            alpha=0.75 if wat_c == wat_order_pca[-1] else 0.5,
            marker=wat_analysis.CLUSTER_MARKERS[wat_c - 1], rasterized=True, linewidths=0)
    wat_ax.set_xlabel(f"PC1 ({wat_s['pca_variance_pc1']:.0%} of variance)")
    wat_ax.set_ylabel(f"PC2 ({wat_s['pca_variance_pc2']:.0%} of variance)")
    wat_leg = wat_ax.legend([wat_handles[wat_c] for wat_c in sorted(wat_handles)],
                            [f"Cluster {wat_c}" for wat_c in sorted(wat_handles)],
                            markerscale=4, loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.0, 1.0), fontsize=14)
    for wat_h in wat_leg.legend_handles:
        wat_h.set_alpha(1)
    wat_f.tight_layout()
    wat_plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Principal component analysis squeezes 9 dimensions into the 2 that keep the most variance:
here PC1 and PC2 keep the shares shown on the axes, so overlaps in the picture can be
separations in the other dimensions. Clusters are numbered by centroid IRCA, from lowest
to highest. The colours pass a colour-vision-deficiency check for every pair on this dark
background and on white pages, and each cluster also has its own marker. The central
cluster is drawn last so the others do not hide it.
:::

## 🌀 Turn the cloud {#water-pca-3d}

```{python}
#| label: wat-cloud
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
# The previous slide's PCA with a third component. This cell computes every number on the
# slide; assets/deck-3d.min.js only draws the points it writes into the page.
import html as wat_html
import json as wat_json
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA as wat_PCA
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors as wat_NN

wat_Z = wat_analysis.zmatrix(wat_res["prepared"])
wat_pca3 = wat_PCA(n_components=3, random_state=wat_analysis.SEED).fit(wat_Z)
wat_xyz = wat_pca3.transform(wat_Z)
# Same first two components as the previous slide, so the cloud starts as that picture.
assert wat_np.allclose(wat_xyz[:, :2], wat_clusters[["pc1", "pc2"]].to_numpy())
wat_var3 = wat_pca3.explained_variance_ratio_
wat_lab = wat_clusters["cluster"].to_numpy()


def wat_same(d):
    """Share of each zone-year's 15 nearest zone-years, on the first d components, in its cluster."""
    # kneighbors() without X leaves each point out, even when another point has its values.
    _, wat_idx = wat_NN(n_neighbors=15).fit(wat_xyz[:, :d]).kneighbors()
    return wat_pd.Series((wat_lab[wat_idx] == wat_lab[:, None]).mean(axis=1))


wat_same2, wat_same3 = wat_same(2), wat_same(3)
wat_own2, wat_own3 = wat_same2.groupby(wat_lab).mean(), wat_same3.groupby(wat_lab).mean()
wat_focus = int(wat_own2.idxmin())  # the cluster most mixed in the 2-D picture
wat_pc3 = wat_pd.Series(wat_pca3.components_[2], index=wat_analysis.FEATURES)
wat_pc3_top = wat_pc3.abs().nlargest(2).index
# Emoji as on the features slide; the words are analysis.py's short labels.
wat_pc3_emoji = {"irca": "💧", "water_coverage": "🚰", "sewer_coverage": "🚽", "ipm": "💸",
                 "rural_share": "🌾", "altitude_m": "⛰️", "rainfall_mm": "🌧️", "mdm": "🏛️",
                 "log_sgp_water_pc": "💰"}


def wat_word(f):
    wat_s = wat_analysis.SHORT_LABELS.get(f, f)
    wat_s = wat_s[0].lower() + wat_s[1:] if wat_s[1:2].islower() else wat_s
    return f"{wat_pc3_emoji.get(f, '')} {wat_s}".strip()


wat_f1, wat_f2 = wat_pc3_top
wat_pc3_text = (("−" if wat_pc3[wat_f1] < 0 else "") + wat_word(wat_f1)
                + (" + " if wat_pc3[wat_f2] > 0 else " − ") + wat_word(wat_f2))
wat_pc3_means = wat_pd.Series(wat_xyz[:, 2]).groupby(wat_lab).mean()
wat_others = wat_pc3_means.drop(wat_focus)
wat_focus_side = ("sits below the others" if wat_pc3_means[wat_focus] < wat_others.min()
                  else "sits above the others" if wat_pc3_means[wat_focus] > wat_others.max()
                  else "moves apart")

wat_cloud = {
    "scale": 100,
    "xyz": wat_np.round(wat_xyz * 100).astype(int).ravel().tolist(),
    "cluster": wat_lab.tolist(),
    "focus": wat_focus,
    # 1st-99th percentiles: the view fits the bulk of the cloud, not its few outliers.
    "lo": wat_np.percentile(wat_xyz, 1, axis=0).round(2).tolist(),
    "hi": wat_np.percentile(wat_xyz, 99, axis=0).round(2).tolist(),
    "clusters": [{"id": int(c), "color": wat_colors[c],
                  "marker": wat_analysis.CLUSTER_MARKERS[c - 1]} for c in sorted(wat_colors)],
}
wat_glyph = {"o": "●", "s": "■", "^": "▲", "D": "◆", "v": "▼", "P": "✚", "X": "✖", "*": "★"}
wat_legend = "".join(
    f'<span><span style="color:{c["color"]}">{wat_glyph.get(c["marker"], "●")}</span> '
    f'Cluster {c["id"]}</span>' for c in wat_cloud["clusters"])
wat_axes = "".join(f'<span class="axis-label">PC{a + 1} · {wat_var3[a]:.0%}</span>' for a in range(3))
wat_alt = (f"Turning 3-D scatter of {len(wat_lab):,} zone-years on the first three principal "
           "components, coloured and shaped by cluster as on the previous slide. Face on it is "
           f"the 2-D picture; turned upright on PC3, cluster {wat_focus} {wat_focus_side}.")
print("```{=html}")
print(f'<div class="deck-3d" data-scene="cloud" role="img" aria-label="{wat_html.escape(wat_alt)}">'
      f'<script type="application/json">{wat_json.dumps(wat_cloud, separators=(",", ":"))}</script>'
      f'<div class="legend">{wat_legend}</div>{wat_axes}'
      '<p class="fallback" hidden>🫧 This 3-D view needs WebGL; the 2-D picture is on '
      'the previous slide.</p></div>')
# The deck's 3-D bundle, loaded once here for this slide and the relief view.
print('<script src="assets/deck-3d.min.js"></script>')
print("```")
```

::: {.steps-3d}
🫧 2 axes · `{python} f"{wat_var3[:2].sum():.0%}"` of variance · cluster `{python} wat_focus`: `{python} f"{wat_own2[wat_focus]:.0%}"` of near neighbours in it

::: {.fragment data-view="turn"}
🔄 3 axes · `{python} f"{wat_var3.sum():.0%}"` · `{python} f"{wat_own3[wat_focus]:.0%}"`
:::

::: {.fragment data-view="pc3"}
PC3 ≈ `{python} wat_pc3_text`: cluster `{python} wat_focus` `{python} wat_focus_side`
:::
:::

[Each point is a zone-year on the first three principal components of the 9 z-scored features, by cluster · 🖱️ drag to turn · scroll to zoom]{.source}

::: {.notes}
The same zone-years, colours and markers as the previous slide, on the first three principal
components of the same 9 z-scored features: PC1 and PC2 are the previous slide's axes.
Face on, the cloud is that 2-D picture. Press → to turn it: PC3 adds `{python} f"{wat_var3[2]:.0%}"` of the variance. Press →
again to stand PC3 upright and fade the other clusters. "Near neighbours" are each
zone-year's 15 nearest zone-years on the components shown; a cluster's share is the mean
over its zone-years. Over all zone-years the share is `{python} f"{wat_same2.mean():.0%}"`
on 2 components and `{python} f"{wat_same3.mean():.0%}"` on 3. PC3's largest
loadings are `{python} ", ".join(f"{f} {wat_pc3[f]:+.2f}" for f in wat_pc3_top)`. It is

## 🏔️ Where the clusters stand {#water-relief}

```{python}
#| label: wat-relief
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
# Columns and borders in km for the relief view; assets/deck-3d.min.js only draws them.
import collections as wat_collections

wat_rel_year = wat_analysis.LAST_YEAR
# The mainland: the San Andrés and Providencia archipelago (department 88) is left off.
wat_rel = wat_clusters[(wat_clusters["zone"] == "urban") & (wat_clusters["year"] == wat_rel_year)
                       & ~wat_clusters["divipola"].str.startswith("88")]
# Heights must be measured altitudes: zones whose altitude prepare() filled are left off.
wat_rel_filled = int(wat_rel["altitude_m_imputed"].sum())
wat_rel = wat_rel[wat_rel["altitude_m_imputed"] == 0]


def wat_part(ring):
    """Area and centroid of a lon/lat ring (shoelace formula)."""
    wat_x, wat_y = ring[:, 0], ring[:, 1]
    wat_c = wat_x * wat_np.roll(wat_y, -1) - wat_np.roll(wat_x, -1) * wat_y
    wat_a = wat_c.sum() / 2
    return (abs(wat_a), (wat_x + wat_np.roll(wat_x, -1)) @ wat_c / (6 * wat_a),
            (wat_y + wat_np.roll(wat_y, -1)) @ wat_c / (6 * wat_a))


# Municipal polygons give each municipality's centroid (of its largest part) and, from the
# edges they share, the borders: an edge of one polygon is the coast or a national
# border; an edge shared across departments is a department border.
wat_centroid, wat_edges, wat_edge_dpts = {}, wat_collections.Counter(), wat_collections.defaultdict(set)
wat_geo = wat_analysis.load_geojson(for_plotly=False)  # read only; the IRCA map reuses it
for wat_feat in wat_geo["features"]:
    wat_code = wat_feat["properties"]["divipola"]
    if wat_code.startswith("88"):
        continue
    wat_gm = wat_feat["geometry"]
    wat_polys = [wat_gm["coordinates"]] if wat_gm["type"] == "Polygon" else wat_gm["coordinates"]
    wat_polys = [[wat_np.asarray(r, dtype=float) for r in p] for p in wat_polys]
    wat_centroid[wat_code] = max((wat_part(p[0]) for p in wat_polys), key=lambda t: t[0])[1:]
    for wat_ring in (r for p in wat_polys for r in p):
        wat_pts = [tuple(v) for v in wat_np.round(wat_ring, 4)]
        for wat_u, wat_v in zip(wat_pts, wat_pts[1:]):
            if wat_u != wat_v:
                wat_e = (wat_u, wat_v) if wat_u < wat_v else (wat_v, wat_u)
                wat_edges[wat_e] += 1
                wat_edge_dpts[wat_e].add(wat_code[:2])
wat_outline = [e for e, n in wat_edges.items() if n == 1]
wat_dpt_edges = [e for e, n in wat_edges.items() if n > 1 and len(wat_edge_dpts[e]) > 1]

# Kilometres from the mainland's centre (equirectangular, fine at Colombia's latitudes).
wat_ll = wat_np.array([p for e in wat_outline for p in e])
wat_lon0, wat_lat0 = (wat_ll.min(0) + wat_ll.max(0)) / 2
wat_kx, wat_ky = 111.32 * wat_np.cos(wat_np.radians(wat_lat0)), 110.57


def wat_km(lon, lat):
    return (lon - wat_lon0) * wat_kx, (lat - wat_lat0) * wat_ky


def wat_segments(edges, step):
    """Border segments snapped to a step-degree grid, as flat km pairs."""
    wat_seen = set()
    for wat_u, wat_v in edges:
        wat_a, wat_b = (tuple(wat_np.round(wat_np.array(p) / step).astype(int)) for p in (wat_u, wat_v))
        if wat_a != wat_b:
            wat_seen.add((wat_a, wat_b) if wat_a < wat_b else (wat_b, wat_a))
    return [round(c) for s in sorted(wat_seen) for p in s for c in wat_km(p[0] * step, p[1] * step)]


wat_exag = 50  # vertical exaggeration: a 3,000 m town stands 150 km tall on the map
wat_xy = wat_np.array([wat_km(*wat_centroid[c]) for c in wat_rel["divipola"]])
wat_alt_med = wat_rel.groupby("cluster")["altitude_m"].median()
wat_high, wat_low = int(wat_alt_med.idxmax()), int(wat_alt_med.idxmin())
# The highest cluster's middle column: the one nearest its median position.
wat_hi_mask = wat_rel["cluster"].to_numpy() == wat_high
wat_hi_cols = wat_xy[wat_hi_mask]
wat_hi_i = wat_np.argmin(((wat_hi_cols - wat_np.median(wat_hi_cols, axis=0)) ** 2).sum(axis=1))
wat_hi_xy, wat_hi_alt = wat_hi_cols[wat_hi_i], wat_rel["altitude_m"].to_numpy()[wat_hi_mask][wat_hi_i]
wat_ext = wat_np.array([wat_km(*p) for p in wat_ll])
wat_relief = {
    "exaggeration": wat_exag,
    "cols": [int(v) for x, y, a, k in zip(wat_xy[:, 0], wat_xy[:, 1], wat_rel["altitude_m"], wat_rel["cluster"])
             for v in (round(x), round(y), round(a), k)],
    "outline": wat_segments(wat_outline, 0.03),
    "departments": wat_segments(wat_dpt_edges, 0.05),
    "extent": [round(v) for v in (wat_ext[:, 0].min(), wat_ext[:, 0].max(), wat_ext[:, 1].min(), wat_ext[:, 1].max())],
    "clusters": [{"id": int(c), "color": wat_colors[c]} for c in sorted(wat_colors)],
    "focus": [wat_high, wat_low],
    # The focus view turns about the highest cluster's middle column, halfway up.
    "view": [round(wat_hi_xy[0]), round(wat_hi_xy[1]), round(wat_hi_alt / 1000 * wat_exag / 2)],
}
# City labels: the ten most populous department capitals (DIVIPOLA codes ending 001) by
# head-town population that year, plus Tunja, among the cities with a column on this map, so
# every label marks a column. Suburbs such as Soacha are left out: their labels would cover
# their capitals'. Each label sits at the top of its city's column; the list is in priority
# order (relief.js hides the last ones first where labels collide), with Tunja, Boyacá's
# capital, second.
wat_towns = wat_raw[(wat_raw["zone"] == "urban") & (wat_raw["year"] == wat_rel_year)
                    & (wat_raw["entity_type"] == "municipality")].set_index("divipola")
wat_col_of = wat_rel.set_index("divipola")[["altitude_m", "cluster"]]
wat_capitals = wat_towns[wat_towns.index.str.endswith("001") & wat_towns.index.isin(wat_col_of.index)]
wat_city_top = list(wat_capitals["population"].nlargest(10).index)
# Tunja must have a column too: a data refresh that drops it fails the render below.
wat_city_codes = wat_city_top[:1] + ["15001"] + [c for c in wat_city_top[1:] if c != "15001"]
# Short names for the four whose official names are long; the rest from `municipio`.
wat_city_names = {"11001": "Bogotá", "76001": "Cali", "13001": "Cartagena", "54001": "Cúcuta"}


def wat_city(c):
    return wat_city_names.get(c, wat_towns.loc[c, "municipio"].title())


wat_relief["cities"] = [
    int(v) for c in wat_city_codes
    for v in (*(round(t) for t in wat_km(*wat_centroid[c])),
              round(wat_col_of.loc[c, "altitude_m"]), wat_col_of.loc[c, "cluster"])]
wat_city_labels = "".join(
    f'<span class="place-label" translate="no">'
    f'{wat_html.escape(wat_city(c))}</span>'
    for c in wat_city_codes)
wat_rel_medians = {c: (f"{wat_alt_med[c]:,.0f} m" if c in wat_alt_med else f"no {wat_rel_year} urban zones")
                   for c in sorted(wat_colors)}
wat_rel_legend = "".join(
    f'<span><span style="color:{wat_colors[c]}">■</span> Cluster {c} · {m}</span>'
    for c, m in wat_rel_medians.items())
wat_rel_alt = (f"3-D map of mainland Colombia with one column for each of the {len(wat_rel)} clustered "
               f"urban zones in {wat_rel_year}, at its municipality's centroid, as tall as its head town's "
               f"altitude and coloured by cluster. Cluster {wat_high}'s columns are the tallest (median "
               f"{wat_alt_med[wat_high]:,.0f} m); cluster {wat_low}'s are the shortest "
               f"({wat_alt_med[wat_low]:,.0f} m). Labels name the ten most populous department "
               "capitals and Tunja.")
wat_region_top = {c: wat_rel.loc[wat_rel["cluster"] == c, "region"].value_counts(normalize=True)
                  for c in (wat_high, wat_low)}
print("```{=html}")
print(f'<div class="deck-3d" data-scene="relief" role="img" aria-label="{wat_html.escape(wat_rel_alt)}">'
      f'<script type="application/json">{wat_json.dumps(wat_relief, separators=(",", ":"))}</script>'
      f'<div class="legend">{wat_rel_legend}</div>{wat_city_labels}'
      '<p class="fallback" hidden>🗺️ This 3-D view needs WebGL. Median head-town altitude, '
      f'{wat_rel_year} urban zones: '
      + "; ".join(f"cluster {c}: {m}" for c, m in wat_rel_medians.items()) + '.</p></div>')
print("```")
```

::: {.steps-3d}
🗺️ `{python} len(wat_rel)` urban zones, `{python} wat_rel_year`: a column each, coloured by cluster

::: {.fragment data-view="tilt"}
⛰️ height = head-town altitude, ×`{python} wat_exag`
:::

::: {.fragment data-view="focus"}
🏔️ cluster `{python} wat_high`: median `{python} f"{wat_alt_med[wat_high]:,.0f}"` m · cluster `{python} wat_low`: `{python} f"{wat_alt_med[wat_low]:,.0f}"` m
:::
:::

[Columns stand at municipality centroids; heights are derived SRTM altitudes of the head towns · labels: the 10 most populous department capitals and Tunja · 🖱️ drag to turn · scroll to zoom]{.source}

::: {.notes}
The previous slide's PC3 ≈ `{python} wat_pc3_text`; this slide puts the clusters on the
map by head-town altitude. One column per clustered urban zone in `{python} wat_rel_year`, at its municipality's
centroid (from the DANE polygons; the head-town coordinates are not in the dataset), as tall
as its head town's altitude (one derived SRTM point, not an official altitude) times

left off`{python} f", and so are {wat_rel_filled} zones whose altitude was filled" if wat_rel_filled else ""`. Press → to tilt the map, and again to fly to cluster `{python} wat_high`, whose
middle column the view turns about; clusters `{python} wat_high` and `{python} wat_low`
stay bright. Cluster `{python} wat_high`'s urban zones are

This shows where the kinds are, not why they differ. The labels name the

and Tunja, Boyacá's capital at `{python} f"{wat_col_of.loc['15001', 'altitude_m']:,.0f}"` m. Large

# 🏷️ Interpret {#water-interpret}

[⏱️ 2:15]{.clock}

## 🌡️ What sets each cluster apart? {#water-heatmap}

```{python}
#| label: fig-wat-heatmap
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Cluster centroids in z units: standard deviations above (red) or below (blue) the year's average. IRCA: utility-supplied (prestadores). Altitude: derived SRTM point."
#| fig-alt: "Heatmap with four rows, clusters 1 to 4, and nine feature columns. Cluster 4 is red for IRCA and poverty and dark blue for water and sewer coverage. Cluster 1 is dark blue for rural share and SGP per person and red for municipal performance. Cluster 3 is dark blue for altitude. Cluster 2 is red for altitude, rural share and coverage."
wat_zcols = [f"z_{wat_c}" for wat_c in wat_analysis.FEATURES]
wat_cmap = wat_LSC.from_list("wat_div", wat_analysis.DIVERGING["dark"])
wat_zlim = 1.5  # colour limit in z; the outcome heatmap uses the same scale
# An example answer for the 💬 check on #water-interpret-page: the highest-IRCA cluster's
# two features farthest from the year's average.
wat_ex_c = int(wat_prof.index.max())
wat_ex = wat_prof.loc[wat_ex_c, wat_zcols].astype(float)
wat_ex = wat_ex[wat_ex.abs().nlargest(2).index]
wat_ex_text = f"cluster {wat_ex_c}: " + " and ".join(
    f"{wat_word(wat_c[2:])} {wat_v:+.1f} SD" for wat_c, wat_v in wat_ex.items())
with wat_plt.rc_context(wat_rc):
    wat_f, wat_ax = wat_plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 0.75 * wat_k + 1.6))
    wat_im = wat_ax.imshow(wat_prof[wat_zcols].to_numpy(), cmap=wat_cmap, vmin=-wat_zlim,
                           vmax=wat_zlim, aspect="auto")
    wat_ax.set_xticks(range(len(wat_zcols)),
                      [wat_analysis.SHORT_LABELS[wat_c] for wat_c in wat_analysis.FEATURES],
                      rotation=25, ha="right")
    wat_ax.set_yticks(range(wat_k), [f"Cluster {wat_c}" for wat_c in wat_prof.index])
    for wat_t, wat_c in zip(wat_ax.get_yticklabels(), wat_prof.index):
        wat_t.set_color(wat_analysis.CLUSTER_TEXT_COLORS["dark"][wat_c - 1])  # ≥ 4.5:1 text
        wat_t.set_fontweight("bold")
    for wat_i, wat_row in enumerate(wat_prof[wat_zcols].to_numpy()):
        for wat_j, wat_v in enumerate(wat_row):
            wat_ax.text(wat_j, wat_i, f"{wat_v:+.1f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=13,
                        color="white")
    wat_ax.spines[:].set_visible(False)
    wat_ax.tick_params(length=0)
    wat_cb = wat_f.colorbar(wat_im, ax=wat_ax, shrink=0.85, pad=0.02)
    wat_cb.set_label("z")
    wat_cb.outline.set_visible(False)
    wat_plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Each cell is the cluster's mean z-score for a feature: +1 means one standard deviation
above that year's average across all kept rows. Read across a row to describe a cluster,
down a column to see which feature separates them. Here, cluster 4 combines high IRCA and
poverty with very low coverage; cluster 3 is low-lying; cluster 1 has low rural share and
high municipal performance; cluster 2 is high, more rural and well served. Cluster labels
use a lighter blue for cluster 1 as text, so every label has at least 4.5:1 contrast.
:::

## 🏷️ Name them by a rule {#water-names}

::: {.bigline}
🏷️ name = 🏙️ setting + 🚰 coverage + 🎚️ median IRCA band
:::

```{python}
#| label: wat-names
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print("| | Kind | Zone-years | Municipalities | Median IRCA |")
print("|---|---|--:|--:|--:|")
for wat_c, wat_p in wat_prof.iterrows():
    print(f'| []{{.wat-swatch style="background:{wat_p["color"]}"}}{wat_c} | {wat_p["name"]} | '
          f'{wat_p["rows"]:,} | {wat_p["municipalities"]:,} | {wat_p["irca_median"]:.1f} |')
print('\n: {tbl-colwidths="[7,45,15,19,14]"}')
```

["low-coverage" = 0.5 SD or more below the year's average, not "unserved" · risk word =
band of the cluster's **median** utility-supplied (prestadores) IRCA, not every zone-year's]{.source}

::: {.notes}
`name_rule()` in `analysis.py` turns each profile into a name, so names never depend on
which id k-means happened to give. Setting: "Rural" if fewer than 40% of the cluster's rows
are urban zones; otherwise "Cities and large towns" (rural share ≤ −0.5 SD), "Lowland towns"
(altitude ≤ −0.5 SD) or "Highland towns" (altitude ≥ +0.5 SD). Coverage: "low-coverage" if
the cluster's mean piped-water coverage is ≤ −0.5 SD. That is a relative position: the rural
cluster's mean coverage is `{python} f"{wat_rural_cov:.0f}"`%, low
but not zero, so "unserved" would overstate it. Risk: the Resolución 2115 band of the
cluster's median utility-supplied (prestadores) IRCA; individual zone-years in a cluster can
sit in any band. Check every name against the heatmap and the profile table before you use
it. Zone-years and
municipalities are counted in `profiles()`; a municipality counts in every cluster that
holds one of its zone-years.
:::

## 🎯 Outcomes by cluster {#water-outcomes}

```{python}
#| label: fig-wat-outcomes
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Median by cluster and year. Infant mortality: 2017–2019 and 2021–2023 only (its method changes in 2017; 2020 looks like another source). Saber 11: published years."
#| fig-alt: "Three small line charts by year, one line per cluster. Cluster 1, cities and large towns, has the lowest infant mortality, around 9 per 1,000, and the highest Saber 11 scores. Cluster 2, highland towns, has the highest infant mortality. Cluster 3, lowland towns, has the lowest Saber 11 scores. Dropout medians stay between about 1.7 and 4.7 percent and dip in 2020 for every cluster."
wat_out = wat_res["outcomes_by_year"]
with wat_plt.rc_context(wat_rc):
    wat_f, wat_axes = wat_plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11.5, 3.25))
    wat_short = {"infant_mortality": "Infant mortality\nper 1,000 births",
                 "saber11_mean": "Saber 11\nmean score", "dropout_rate": "School dropout\n(%)"}
    for wat_ax, wat_col in zip(wat_axes, wat_analysis.OUTCOMES):
        wat_o = wat_out[wat_out["outcome"] == wat_col]
        for wat_c, wat_g in wat_o.groupby("cluster"):
            # Every year of the span: excluded years become gaps, not joined lines.
            wat_yrs = wat_analysis.OUTCOME_YEARS[wat_col]
            wat_g = wat_g.set_index("year").reindex(range(min(wat_yrs), max(wat_yrs) + 1))
            wat_ax.plot(wat_g.index, wat_g["median"], marker=wat_analysis.CLUSTER_MARKERS[wat_c - 1],
                        markersize=7, color=wat_colors[wat_c], label=f"{wat_c} · {wat_names[wat_c]}")
        wat_ax.set_title(wat_short[wat_col], fontsize=15, loc="left")
        wat_ax.set_xticks([2016, 2019, 2022])
        wat_ax.tick_params(labelsize=14)
    wat_f.legend(*wat_axes[0].get_legend_handles_labels(), loc="lower center", ncol=2,
                 fontsize=14, bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.24), columnspacing=1.5)
    wat_f.tight_layout(w_pad=2)
    wat_plt.show()
```

[⚠️ Descriptive only: these differences are not causal effects of water quality. Infant
mortality and dropout are municipal values.]{.source}

::: {.notes}
Medians within each year, so the comparison never mixes years. Infant mortality changes
method in 2017 and 2020 looks like another source (data README, caveat 8), so only
2017–2019 and 2021–2023 are drawn; from 2017 a blank may mean no recorded deaths, and small
municipalities produce extreme rates. Saber 11 is missing in 2018, 2021 and 2023. Infant
mortality and dropout are measured for the whole municipality but repeated on both zone
rows: an ecological mismatch with the zone-level clusters. The highland-town result is a
good discussion point: these are small municipalities, where rates are noisy.
:::

## 🌡️ Outcomes in SD units {#water-outcome-heatmap}

```{python}
#| label: fig-wat-outcome-heatmap
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Cluster mean outcome in z units (SD above red, below blue the year's average); the mean itself in brackets. Colour scale as in the features heatmap."
#| fig-alt: "Heatmap with one row per cluster and three outcome columns: infant mortality, Saber 11 and school dropout. Each cell prints the cluster's mean outcome in z units and, in brackets, the mean itself, coloured on the features heatmap's blue-to-red scale."
# Like the features: standardise within year, then average over each cluster's rows.
# Municipal outcomes count each municipality once per year (or cluster), as in profiles().
wat_ocols = list(wat_analysis.OUTCOMES)
wat_oz = {}
for wat_col in wat_ocols:
    wat_r = wat_clusters[wat_clusters["year"].isin(wat_analysis.OUTCOME_YEARS[wat_col])]
    wat_r = wat_r.dropna(subset=[wat_col])
    wat_base = (wat_r.drop_duplicates(["divipola", "year"])
                if wat_analysis.OUTCOME_LEVEL[wat_col] == "municipality" else wat_r)
    wat_mu = wat_base.groupby("year")[wat_col].mean()
    wat_sd = wat_base.groupby("year")[wat_col].std(ddof=0)
    wat_r = wat_analysis.once_per_municipality(wat_r, wat_col)
    wat_z = (wat_r[wat_col] - wat_r["year"].map(wat_mu)) / wat_r["year"].map(wat_sd)
    wat_oz[wat_col] = wat_z.groupby(wat_r["cluster"]).mean()
wat_oz = wat_pd.DataFrame(wat_oz).loc[wat_prof.index]
wat_ohead = {"infant_mortality": "Infant mortality\nper 1,000 · ↓ better",
             "saber11_mean": "Saber 11\nscore · ↑ better",
             "dropout_rate": "Dropout\n% · ↓ better"}
wat_ofmt = {"infant_mortality": "{:.1f}", "saber11_mean": "{:.0f}", "dropout_rate": "{:.1f}%"}
wat_omean = wat_prof[[f"{wat_c}_mean" for wat_c in wat_ocols]]
wat_oname = {wat_c: f"cluster {wat_c} ({wat_names[wat_c].split(',')[0].lower()})"
             for wat_c in wat_prof.index}
wat_ozmax = f"{wat_oz.abs().to_numpy().max():.2f}"
with wat_plt.rc_context(wat_rc):
    wat_f, wat_ax = wat_plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 0.65 * wat_k + 1.3))
    wat_im = wat_ax.imshow(wat_oz.to_numpy(), cmap=wat_cmap, vmin=-wat_zlim, vmax=wat_zlim,
                           aspect="auto")
    wat_ax.set_xticks(range(len(wat_ocols)), [wat_ohead[wat_c] for wat_c in wat_ocols])
    wat_ax.xaxis.tick_top()
    wat_ax.set_yticks(range(wat_k), [f"Cluster {wat_c}" for wat_c in wat_prof.index])
    for wat_t, wat_c in zip(wat_ax.get_yticklabels(), wat_prof.index):
        wat_t.set_color(wat_analysis.CLUSTER_TEXT_COLORS["dark"][wat_c - 1])  # ≥ 4.5:1 text
        wat_t.set_fontweight("bold")
    for wat_i, wat_c in enumerate(wat_prof.index):
        for wat_j, wat_col in enumerate(wat_ocols):
            wat_mean = wat_ofmt[wat_col].format(wat_prof.loc[wat_c, f"{wat_col}_mean"])
            wat_ax.text(wat_j, wat_i, f"{wat_oz.loc[wat_c, wat_col]:+.2f}  ({wat_mean})",
                        ha="center", va="center", fontsize=14, color="white")
    wat_ax.spines[:].set_visible(False)
    wat_ax.tick_params(length=0)
    wat_cb = wat_f.colorbar(wat_im, ax=wat_ax, shrink=0.85, pad=0.02)
    wat_cb.set_label("z")
    wat_cb.outline.set_visible(False)
    wat_plt.show()
```

[⚠️ Descriptive only: not causal effects of water quality. Infant mortality: 2017–2019 and
2021–2023; Saber 11: published years.]{.source}

::: {.notes}
The same recipe as the features heatmap: each outcome is standardised within its year
(value minus that year's mean, divided by that year's standard deviation), and a cell is
the cluster's mean z, with the cluster's mean outcome in brackets. Municipal outcomes
(infant mortality, dropout) count each municipality once per year for the year's mean and
standard deviation, and once per cluster and year inside a cluster, as `profiles()` does.
Years: infant mortality 2017–2019 and 2021–2023, Saber 11 2016, 2017, 2019, 2020 and 2022,
dropout 2016–2023. The colour scale is the features heatmap's (±`{python} wat_zlim`), so the
paler cells are the point: no cluster's mean outcome is more than `{python} wat_ozmax` SD
from the average, and the clusters differ far less in outcomes than in the features that
formed them. Lowest infant mortality:
`{python} wat_oname[wat_omean["infant_mortality_mean"].idxmin()]`; highest:
`{python} wat_oname[wat_omean["infant_mortality_mean"].idxmax()]`. Best Saber 11:
`{python} wat_oname[wat_omean["saber11_mean_mean"].idxmax()]`. Lowest dropout:
`{python} wat_oname[wat_omean["dropout_rate_mean"].idxmin()]`.
:::

## 🎛️ Every variable, cluster by cluster {#water-compare}

```{python}
#| label: wat-compare
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
# One box-plot image per feature and outcome; a plain menu shows one at a time, so the
# slide needs no extra library and works offline.
import base64 as wat_b64
import html as wat_html
import io as wat_io
import textwrap as wat_textwrap

wat_vars = {**{wat_c: wat_analysis.FEATURE_LABELS[wat_c] for wat_c in wat_analysis.FEATURES},
            **wat_analysis.OUTCOMES}
wat_ids = list(wat_prof.index)
wat_opts, wat_imgs = [], []
for wat_i, (wat_col, wat_lab) in enumerate(wat_vars.items()):
    wat_r = wat_clusters
    if wat_col in wat_analysis.OUTCOMES:
        wat_r = wat_r[wat_r["year"].isin(wat_analysis.OUTCOME_YEARS[wat_col])]
        wat_r = wat_analysis.once_per_municipality(wat_r.dropna(subset=[wat_col]), wat_col)
    wat_vals = [wat_r.loc[wat_r["cluster"] == wat_c, wat_col].dropna().to_numpy()
                for wat_c in wat_ids]
    with wat_plt.rc_context(wat_rc):
        wat_f, wat_ax = wat_plt.subplots(figsize=(10.5, 4.4))
        wat_bp = wat_ax.boxplot(wat_vals, whis=(5, 95), showfliers=False, showmeans=True,
                                meanline=True, patch_artist=True, widths=0.5,
                                medianprops=dict(color="#f0f0f0", linewidth=2.5),
                                meanprops=dict(color="#f0f0f0", linestyle="--", linewidth=1.8))
        for wat_j, wat_c in enumerate(wat_ids):
            wat_bp["boxes"][wat_j].set(facecolor=wat_colors[wat_c] + "80",
                                       edgecolor=wat_colors[wat_c], linewidth=2)
            for wat_part in ("whiskers", "caps"):
                for wat_line in wat_bp[wat_part][2 * wat_j:2 * wat_j + 2]:
                    wat_line.set(color=wat_colors[wat_c], linewidth=2)
        # Break each name before its risk word; the rural name has two commas.
        wat_ax.set_xticks(range(1, len(wat_ids) + 1),
                          [",\n".join(wat_names[wat_c].rsplit(", ", 1)) for wat_c in wat_ids],
                          fontsize=13)
        for wat_t, wat_c in zip(wat_ax.get_xticklabels(), wat_ids):
            wat_t.set_color(wat_analysis.CLUSTER_TEXT_COLORS["dark"][wat_c - 1])
        wat_ax.set_ylabel("\n".join(wat_textwrap.wrap(wat_lab, 26)))
        wat_ax.yaxis.grid(True, color="#3a3a3a")
        wat_ax.set_axisbelow(True)
        wat_buf = wat_io.BytesIO()
        wat_f.savefig(wat_buf, format="png", bbox_inches="tight")
        wat_plt.close(wat_f)
    wat_src = wat_b64.b64encode(wat_buf.getvalue()).decode()
    wat_alt = (f"Box plots of {wat_lab}, one per cluster. Medians: "
               + "; ".join(f"cluster {wat_c} {wat_np.median(wat_v):.1f}"
                           if len(wat_v) else f"cluster {wat_c} no data"
                           for wat_c, wat_v in zip(wat_ids, wat_vals)) + ".")
    wat_opts.append(f'<option value="{wat_i}">{wat_html.escape(wat_lab)}</option>')
    wat_imgs.append(f'<img data-i="{wat_i}" alt="{wat_html.escape(wat_alt)}" '
                    f'src="data:image/png;base64,{wat_src}"'
                    + (' style="display:none"' if wat_i else "") + ">")
print("```{=html}")
print('<div class="wat-compare"><select aria-label="Variable" '
      'onkeydown="event.stopPropagation()" onchange="for (const im of '
      "this.parentNode.querySelectorAll('img')) im.style.display = "
      "im.dataset.i === this.value ? '' : 'none'\">" + "".join(wat_opts) + "</select>"
      + "".join(wat_imgs) + "</div>")
print("```")
```

[▭ middle half · ━ median · ┅ mean · whiskers 5th–95th percentile · all zone-years
2016–2023; outcomes in their years, municipal ones once per municipality]{.source}

::: {.notes}
Pick a variable in the menu: the boxes show how its values spread within each cluster, so
the overlaps are visible as well as the gaps between means. Features are the values that
went into the clustering, after imputation (`water_coverage` and `sewer_coverage` medians
filled `{python} f"{wat_s['imputed_water_coverage']:,}"` and
`{python} f"{wat_s['imputed_sewer_coverage']:,}"` rows); outcomes were never clustered on.
Each variable is a small image drawn by this deck, and the menu only shows one at a time,
so the slide needs no plotting library in the browser and works offline. The arrow keys
change the menu's choice while it has focus; click the slide to move on. It is descriptive:
a gap between clusters is not an effect of water quality.
:::

# ⚠️ Correlation ≠ causation {#water-causation}

[⏱️ 2:30]{.clock}

## 📉 Worse water, more infant deaths? {#water-within}

```{python}
#| label: fig-wat-within
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Median infant mortality by utility-supplied (prestadores) IRCA band, per cluster. Infant mortality changes method in 2017, and 2020 looks like another source: 2017–2019 and 2021–2023 are pooled. Bands under 20 municipality-years are not drawn."
#| fig-alt: "Four small panels, one per cluster, each showing median infant mortality across the five IRCA risk bands, labelled N, L, M, H and U for no risk, low, medium, high and unfit. The lines are nearly flat in every cluster, and the Spearman correlations printed on the panels are all close to zero."
wat_rho = wat_res["irca_infant"].set_index("cluster")
wat_bins = wat_res["irca_infant_bins"]
wat_bins = wat_bins[wat_bins["n"] >= 20]
wat_rho_lo = f"{wat_rho['spearman_rho'].min():+.2f}"
wat_rho_hi = f"{wat_rho['spearman_rho'].max():+.2f}"
with wat_plt.rc_context(wat_rc):
    wat_f, wat_axes = wat_plt.subplots(1, wat_k, figsize=(11.5, 3.2), sharey=True)
    for wat_ax, (wat_c, wat_g) in zip(wat_axes, wat_bins.groupby("cluster")):
        wat_pos = [wat_analysis.IRCA_BANDS.index(wat_b) for wat_b in wat_g["irca_band"]]
        wat_ax.plot(wat_pos, wat_g["median"], marker=wat_analysis.CLUSTER_MARKERS[wat_c - 1],
                    markersize=8, color=wat_colors[wat_c])
        wat_ax.set_title(f"Cluster {wat_c}", fontsize=15, loc="left", fontweight="bold",
                         color=wat_analysis.CLUSTER_TEXT_COLORS["dark"][wat_c - 1])
        wat_ax.text(0.04, 0.05, f"ρ = {wat_rho.loc[wat_c, 'spearman_rho']:+.2f}\n"
                    f"n = {wat_rho.loc[wat_c, 'n']:,}", transform=wat_ax.transAxes, fontsize=14)
        wat_ax.set_xticks(range(5), ["N", "L", "M", "H", "U"], fontsize=14)
        wat_ax.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=14)
    wat_axes[0].set_ylim(0, wat_bins["median"].max() * 1.3)
    wat_axes[0].set_ylabel("Infant mortality\nper 1,000", fontsize=14)
    wat_f.supxlabel("IRCA band:  N no risk · L low · M medium · H high · U unfit", fontsize=14)
    wat_f.tight_layout()
    wat_plt.show()
```

::: {.bigline}
⚠️ descriptive only: **not** a causal effect of water quality
:::

::: {.notes}
Spearman's ρ within each cluster is between `{python} wat_rho_lo` and `{python} wat_rho_hi` (computed by
`irca_vs_infant()`; n = municipality-years with both values, a municipality whose two zones
share a cluster counted once with their mean IRCA). A flat line does not show that water
is harmless either: the outcome is municipal while IRCA is zonal, blank rates (which may
mean zero deaths) are left out, small municipalities have noisy rates, and confounders
push in both directions. The binned medians follow the Resolución 2115 bands.
:::

## 🤔 What else could explain it? {#water-confounders}

::: {.cards style="grid-template-columns: repeat(5, 1fr);"}
::: {}
[💸]{.big}

**poverty**
:::
::: {.fragment}
[🌾]{.big}

**rurality**
:::
::: {.fragment}
[🏥]{.big}

**health-service access**
:::
::: {.fragment}
[📝]{.big}

**reporting quality**
:::
::: {.fragment}
[🔍]{.big}

**ecological level**: municipal outcome, zone IRCA
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Confounders affect both water quality and health: poorer and more rural places have worse
water and worse access to clinics, and they also register fewer births and deaths. The
ecological fallacy: a pattern across places need not hold for the people in them. Clusters
hold some of this constant, but not all: within a cluster, places still differ in poverty
and access. A causal claim would need a design that handles these, such as before/after
changes in treatment plants with comparison places.
:::

## ✍️🌐 2:55 · Blog + website {#water-website}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{.yaml}
# _quarto.yml
project:
  type: website
  execute-dir: project
  pre-render: scripts/analysis.py
execute:
  freeze: false
```
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
```{.yaml}
# index.qmd
listing:
  contents: posts
```

🔁 `pre-render` rebuilds `outputs/`

🧪 `freeze: false` re-runs **every** page → always the new numbers
:::
::::

::: {.fragment}
⭐ later, for slow sites: `freeze: auto` reuses old results\
until you run `rm -rf _freeze`
:::

::: {.notes}
`pre-render` runs the script before every render, including a single-file render inside
the project. `freeze: false` re-executes every page on every render, so one `uv run quarto render`
rebuilds the analysis and every publication, and nothing needs clearing when `data/` or the
script change. `execute-dir: project` makes every page, including the post in `posts/…/`,
read `outputs/` and `data/` from the project folder. Optional extension for slow sites:
`freeze: auto` stores each page's results in `_freeze/` and re-executes a page only when its
own source changes, so changes to `data/` or `outputs/` are not detected; delete `_freeze/`
(or render that page directly, which ignores freeze) after the data or the analysis change.
A listing turns `posts/*/index.qmd` into a blog index.
Docs: https://quarto.org/docs/projects/scripts.html,
https://quarto.org/docs/projects/code-execution.html#freeze,

## 📈 3:05 · Dashboard {#water-dashboard}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-wat-map
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Urban zones, 2023: utility-supplied (prestadores) IRCA band."
#| fig-alt: "Map of Colombia's municipalities coloured by the 2023 IRCA band of their head town, with a legend from hatched no data through no risk, low, medium and high to unfit. Most of the Andean interior is in the darker no-risk and low-risk colours, scattered municipalities are bright high-risk, and much of the east and the Amazon is hatched for no data."
# wat_geo: the municipal polygons, read by the relief view's cell (#water-relief).
wat_last_year = wat_analysis.LAST_YEAR
wat_urban = wat_clusters[(wat_clusters["zone"] == "urban") & (wat_clusters["year"] == wat_last_year)]
wat_band_of = dict(zip(wat_urban["divipola"], wat_urban["irca_band"].astype(str)))
wat_band_col = dict(zip(wat_analysis.IRCA_BANDS, wat_analysis.BAND_COLORS["dark"]))
wat_polys, wat_fill, wat_nodata_polys = [], [], []
for wat_feat in wat_geo["features"]:
    wat_gm = wat_feat["geometry"]
    wat_parts = [wat_gm["coordinates"]] if wat_gm["type"] == "Polygon" else wat_gm["coordinates"]
    wat_col = wat_band_col.get(wat_band_of.get(wat_feat["properties"]["divipola"]))
    for wat_part in wat_parts:
        if wat_col is None:               # no data: hatched, so it never reads as a band
            wat_nodata_polys.append(wat_np.asarray(wat_part[0]))
        else:
            wat_polys.append(wat_np.asarray(wat_part[0]))
            wat_fill.append(wat_col)
wat_nodata_style = dict(facecolor=wat_analysis.NO_DATA_COLOR["dark"],
                        edgecolor=wat_analysis.NO_DATA_EDGE["dark"],
                        hatch=wat_analysis.NO_DATA_HATCH)
wat_legend = ([wat_plt.Rectangle((0, 0), 1, 1, linewidth=0, **wat_nodata_style)]
              + [wat_plt.Rectangle((0, 0), 1, 1, color=wat_c)
                 for wat_c in wat_analysis.BAND_COLORS["dark"]])
with wat_plt.rc_context(wat_rc):
    wat_f, wat_ax = wat_plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.6))
    wat_ax.add_collection(wat_PolyCollection(wat_nodata_polys, linewidths=0.15,
                                             **wat_nodata_style))
    wat_ax.add_collection(wat_PolyCollection(wat_polys, facecolors=wat_fill,
                                             edgecolors="#191919", linewidths=0.15))
    wat_ax.set_xlim(-84.5, -66.7)
    wat_ax.set_ylim(-4.4, 12.6)
    wat_ax.set_aspect("equal")
    wat_ax.axis("off")
    wat_ax.legend(wat_legend, ["no data"] + [wat_b.lower() for wat_b in wat_analysis.IRCA_BANDS],
                  loc="lower left", fontsize=13, handlelength=1, borderaxespad=0)
    wat_f.tight_layout(pad=0)
    wat_plt.show()
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
🗺️ choropleth: `municipios.geojson` joined on `divipola`

🎚️ year slider: `{python} wat_analysis.FIRST_YEAR` → `{python} wat_last_year`

🔎 search a department → its municipalities

🗂️ two pages: map · table
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
The map on the slide is a static preview drawn by this deck from the GeoJSON and the
clustered rows (urban zones, 2023; hatched = no value or not clustered, so it never reads
as the lowest band; Providencia is off the top edge). In the dashboard, Plotly draws it
interactively. Two
traps: the GeoJSON follows RFC 7946 (exterior rings counter-clockwise), and Plotly expects
the opposite winding, so without reversing the rings every municipality is drawn as "the
world minus the municipality" (a grey rectangle). And animation frames should update only
`z`: if each year repeats the 2.7 MB geometry, the HTML balloons. Dashboard layout and
components: https://quarto.org/docs/dashboards/ (checked 2026-10-30).
:::

::: {.source .behind}

```
:::

::: {.done}
the dashboard has Map, Kinds, Outcomes, Method and Municipalities pages.
:::

::: {.notes}
Compute once, publish many: every new page reads files `analysis.py` already wrote, so the
dashboard never recomputes a number. A level-1 heading starts a dashboard page
(https://quarto.org/docs/dashboards/layout.html#pages, checked 2026-10-31). With Quarto
1.6.40 a dashboard cell shows every top-level expression, not only the last one: a bare
`fig.add_vline(...)` line draws the chart a second time, so assign it (`fig = fig.add_vline(...)`)
and end the cell with `fig`. If legend entries overlap, ask for a horizontal legend with a
fixed `entrywidth`; years without data should stay gaps, not joined lines. Optional and
self-paced: not counted in the agenda's exercise times.
The finished dashboard is `quarto-workshop/examples/water/dashboard.qmd`.
:::

::: {.source .behind}
😰 Stuck?

Catch me up: follow ../quarto-workshop/examples/water/README.md
```
:::

::: {.done}
`https://<your-github-username>.github.io/water-quality/` opens in a browser.
:::

::: {.notes}
Same steps as Part 1. The assistant runs `gh repo create water-quality --public --source=.
--push` with the `gh` sign-in from the setup check (https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_repo_create).
`quarto publish gh-pages --no-prompt` skips the confirmation question an assistant cannot
answer (`quarto publish --help`, Quarto 1.6.40); it renders locally (running the pre-render
script), creates the `gh-pages` branch on its first run, pushes `_site/` and opens the site.
A project site needs no Settings → Pages change; that page only shows the URL and status.
Docs: https://quarto.org/docs/publishing/github-pages.html (checked 2026-10-30). The data is public (CC BY-SA 4.0 and CC BY 4.0 sources, see
`data/README.md`), so publishing `data/` with the site is fine; keep the attributions. The 💬
check is the workshop's lesson in one question: `scripts/analysis.py` for a method choice
(or `data/` for new data); `pre-render` re-runs it and `freeze: false` re-runs every page,
so one `uv run quarto render` updates the report, slides, blog and dashboard together.
:::

::: {.notes}
Sankey: count municipalities' zones by cluster in 2016 and 2023 (Plotly `go.Sankey`).
Positive deviants: zone-years in the rural high-risk cluster with low infant mortality and
high Saber 11; visit their stories. GMM gives each row a probability per cluster; HDBSCAN
finds dense groups and leaves outliers unclustered. Under-5 diarrhoeal disease (EDA)
incidence is not in the open SIVIGILA data, which publishes only EDA deaths
(https://portalsivigila.ins.gov.co/; data README, TODO 2).
:::

  data [doi:10.15780/G2JQ0P](https://doi.org/10.15780/G2JQ0P); Funk et al. (2015),
